The problem with inaccuracy with the M1911 style autos is that the axis of the bore moves independent of the sights on the top of the slide. Many places sell genuine colt National Match Barrels, Bushings and links with a drop in fit. While these may help your accuracy they won't give you the tack driving accuracy of a true match weapon.

If you want a tack driver a few minutes with a Wire feed TIG welder and a lot of time with files and abrasive stones are required.

The first thing you want to do is extend the length and width of the tang at the top of the chamber of the barre. This shouldn't cause much heat distortion of the barre because the tang extends from the top rear of the chamber and is totally surround by air. If you want to make sure your barrel is not damaged by heat stand it muzzle down in water up to the chamber. The next area that you want to build up is the ramp under the barrel. Again place the barrel in water about 3/4 the way up the barrel to the ramp add metal to the ramp. Lastly add metal to the inside and out side [of the busing and to the lug that engages the slot in side the slide.

Now that you got the critical areas of the barrel and bushing built up start the fitting process. The first thing to do is fit the busing to the slide. The first thing you want to do is wedge the busing onto a piece of wood and chuck up in a drill. Rotate the barrel busing and using a thin abrasive stone grind away the outer circumference until it will fit tightly into the slide. Once you have the bushing fitted there will be excess metal around the barrel bushing retaining lug. Use fine Swiss patter files to dimension the lug to where it will rotate into retaining slot with great difficulty. Also the bushing must fit flat against the face of the slide. Use some mechanics bluing to check the fit. Put a very thin coat of bluing on the slide install the busing and then remove. You should see a solid transfer from the slide to the bushing. (Most national Match weapons are never disassembled or if they are there is a special wrench that is used to turn the barrel bushing.)

Next we need to fit the barrel to the bushing. National Match barrels have a built up ring around the muzzle that engages the bushing when in the slide is in battery. Most commercial barrels do not. What you want to do is us a wooden dowel and chuck the barrel up in a drill. Use a flat wide and thin wooden stick with abrasive paper glued to it. Rotate the barrel and using the abrasive paper remove about .002-.;005 from the barrel from about 1/4 inch back from the muzzle all the way back to the barrel tang. This is to give clearance so the slide will recoil easily once it as unseated from the barrel. Remember the barrel must tilt downward to unlock from the slide but you do not want any movement between the barrel and the bushing when the barrel is locked to the slide. You should be able to see the muzzle band with the naked eye and barely feel the step with your finger.

Next we fit the bushing to the barrel. THIS IS A MOST TIME CONSUMING STEP. A good dial caliper is mandatory here. You now must remove the excess metal from the inside of the barrel busing. The best way to do this is place the bushing into a rubber short length of rubber hose with a stick in the other end. Mount the stick in a drill and start rotating the busing. Use a round Swiss patter file the rough the barrel busing down to about .01" undersized.. (The barrel should not got into the bushing at this point.) Now change to some abrasive paper wrapped around a 3/8 dowel and continue to remove metal from the inside of the barrel bushing. (Stop frequently to check barrel to bushing fit. yes you can push the barrel through the bushing from the front.) Keep checking until the barrel will go through the bushing with force. Now use 400 grit abrasive paper on the dowel to bring the barrel bushing down to size. When the barrel will slide easily into the bushing, but when you have the bushing slid all the way down the barrel, and you hold the muzzle end of the barrel in gripped in your hand for 5-10 seconds, the heat from your hand should expand the barrel sufficiently so that when you hold the bushing the barrel will be suspended from the busing and not slide through until it cools down.

Now we have the bushing fitted to the slide and the barrel fitted to the bushing.

The next step is fitting the tang at the top rear of the barrel to the slot at the rear of the ejection port of the slide. The object here is to have tang just short enough and narrow enough to allow the barrel to lock in the slide. You are there when you put a very thin coating of mechanics blueing on the tang at the top of the barrel. and when barrel locks into the slide you should get a solid transfer of bluing onto ejection port slot of the slide.

The last step is the re profiling of the barrel link tang so when the barrel is locked to the slide the link tang is resting firmly on the barrel link pin. By proper profiling of the barrel link tang you can slightly control how far the barrel will travel before it becomes unlocked from the slide. If done right the barrel slide will travel sufficient distance to pull the barrel busing off its mating surface on the barrel before the barrel starts to tilt to unlock.

Once you have done all the above you should really tighten your grouping. The only down side of doing all this stuff is the gun will now be a lot more sensitive to dirt and crud.
